author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the propagation and exfiltration stage
of the "Miasma" / "Phantom Gyp" npm supply-chain worm (StepSecurity + Snyk
disclosure, 2026-06-03). After the `binding.gyp` code-execution stage
(related rule `observed_miasma_binding_gyp_command_substitution_t1195_002`)
harvests npm/GitHub/cloud credentials, the worm uses the stolen GitHub
token two ways:

(1) Self-propagation: injects a commit into any reachable GitHub Actions
workflow via the GitHub GraphQL API's `createCommitOnBranch` mutation
(POST to `api.github.com/graphql`) -- not a plain `git push`, which is
the detection-relevant distinction, since it lets the worm commit through
the API using only a stolen token, without a local git working tree.

(2) Exfiltration: stolen secrets are RSA-encrypted and uploaded as JSON
(`results/results-{timestamp}.json`) to newly created private GitHub
repos under a single controller account (`liuende501`, ~236 repos
observed), named from two fixed theme sets that StepSecurity documents
verbatim: Dune terms (`atreides`, `fedaykin`, `sardaukar`, `tleilaxu`) and
Greek-mythology terms (`nemean-hydra`, `cerberus`, `chimera`), several
suffixed with a random numeric ID (e.g. `nemean-hydra-34343`) -- a naming
convention distinctive enough to key on, not a generic "random repo name"
claim.

Detection logic requires BOTH an npm-install-lineage process (so a
developer's own unrelated GitHub scripting does not fire this alone) AND
one of the two campaign-specific signals (the GraphQL mutation name, or
the exfil path/repo-naming pattern) -- the naming-pattern half is
inherently weaker evidence than the mutation-name half (a coincidental
hit on "cerberus" as a legitimate repo name is plausible on its own),
which is why this rule is `level: medium` rather than `high` unlike its
two sibling rules in this cluster, and why the process-lineage condition
is required rather than optional.

Aggregated from 2 independent technical disclosures, 2026-06-03/04
(StepSecurity, Snyk).
falsepositives: A repo or automation script that legitimately uses GitHub's GraphQL API and the `createCommitOnBranch` mutation for its own CI/bot purposes -- the npm-install-lineage condition narrows this, but does not eliminate a CI pipeline that happens to both install npm packages and push commits via GraphQL in the same job

A coincidental match on one of the theme words (e.g. a legitimately named `cerberus-monitoring` repo referenced in a build script) -- this half of the rule is deliberately weaker evidence, hence the medium severity level rather than high; do not treat a hit on naming alone as high-confidence without the mutation-name signal or external corroboration
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=1 AND ((ParentImage LIKE '%\\npm.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\npm.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\npm-cli.js' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\pnpm.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\pnpm.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\yarn.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\yarn.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\bun.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND (CommandLine LIKE '%createCommitOnBranch%' ESCAPE '\' OR (CommandLine LIKE '%results/results-%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%nemean-hydra%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%atreides%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%fedaykin%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%sardaukar%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%tleilaxu%' ESCAPE '\'))))
title: Miasma npm worm -- T1567.001 GitHub GraphQL commit injection + themed-repo credential exfiltration

author: WRG-11
description:
Detects a Windows scripting host resolving the Google Gemini API host
(generativelanguage.googleapis.com). Google Threat Intelligence Group
(GTIG) reports AI-augmented malware families that call the Gemini API at
runtime instead of shipping their evasion logic statically: PROMPTFLUX, a
VBScript dropper that sends a POST request to the Gemini API with a
hard-coded key and asks the model to rewrite its own source code, and
HONESTCUE, which requests VBScript obfuscation and evasion techniques from
the Gemini API for just-in-time self-modification.

GTIG does not attribute either family to a named threat actor; the
November 2025 report notes PROMPTFLUX filenames suggest financially
motivated operators. This rule is therefore keyed on the behaviour, not on
an actor.

Legitimate Gemini integrations resolve the same host, so the rule narrows
on the resolving process: wscript, cscript and mshta resolving a hosted
LLM API are uncommon in benign software. PowerShell and the LOLBin hosts
are included because they are common launchers for the same script
payloads, and are the main false-positive surface.
falsepositives: Administrative automation that calls the Gemini API from a PowerShell script; allowlist the specific script path or signed automation account.
Internal AI tooling packaged behind a scripting host; confirm the resolving binary and its parent before alerting.
Red-team tooling exercising LLM API endpoints during an authorised engagement.
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=22 AND (QueryName LIKE '%generativelanguage.googleapis.com' ESCAPE '\' AND (Image LIKE '%\\wscript.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\cscript.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\mshta.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\pwsh.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\regsvr32.exe' ESCAPE '\')))
title: PROMPTFLUX / HONESTCUE pattern -- Gemini API resolved by a scripting host -- T1102.002

Anything executed over WinRM on the receiving host is a child of wsmprovhost.exe, the WinRM provider host -- so the parent process, not the command line, is what identifies remote execution. That makes this a reliable lateral-movement signal on hosts where WinRM is not the sanctioned administration path, and near-useless noise on hosts where it is; scope by asset role before deploying. Synthetic exemplar from the WinstonRedGuard threat-intel corpus -- no actor binding; review and bind to your environment before deployment.
falsepositives: Configuration management that uses WinRM as its transport (DSC, Ansible on Windows, PowerShell Remoting-based tooling) -- on those estates this fires constantly and by design

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the persistence stage of the "Miasma"
/ "Phantom Gyp" npm supply-chain worm (StepSecurity + Snyk disclosure,
2026-06-03). This is the standout TTP of the campaign and, as of this
rule's authoring, not covered by any other rule in this corpus: instead
of (or in addition to) classic host persistence, the worm writes
auto-executing configuration files into every AI-assisted IDE/agent
integration it can find in the poisoned project tree, so the backdoor
re-fires the next time a developer opens the project with an AI coding
tool:

- Claude Code: `.claude/setup.mjs` (session-start hook) and
  `.claude/settings.json`
- Cursor: `.cursor/rules/setup.mdc` (fires on project-open)
- Google Gemini: `.gemini/settings.json`
- VS Code: `.vscode/tasks.json` (`runOn: folderOpen`) and
  `.vscode/setup.mjs`
- GitHub Actions: `.github/setup.js`

Both source blogs independently list this same file-path set (StepSecurity
names all six; Snyk corroborates the Claude/Cursor/VS Code subset). The
social-engineering cover text embedded in the poisoned project reads
"This is required for proper IDE integration and dependency setup." The
payload files execute via the Bun runtime rather than Node, for the same
process-tree evasion reason as the initial `binding.gyp` stage (related
rule: `observed_miasma_binding_gyp_command_substitution_t1195_002`).

Detection logic flags the creation of any of these six specific,
auto-executing AI-tool config paths inside a project directory,
attributed to a process descending from an npm-family package manager
(i.e. written during/after `npm install`, not hand-authored by the
developer in an editor) -- a developer manually adding one of these files
themselves is a normal, high-volume event this rule must not fire on,
so the process-lineage condition is load-bearing, not decorative.

Mapped to T1546 (Event Triggered Execution) at the parent-technique level:
none of the existing sub-techniques (change-default-file-association,
screensaver, etc.) describes "an AI coding assistant's own project-open
hook", so this rule does not force a sub-technique that does not fit
rather than making one up.

Aggregated from 2 independent technical disclosures, 2026-06-03/04
(StepSecurity, Snyk).
falsepositives: A developer or scaffolding tool legitimately creating one of these files by hand (e.g. `.vscode/tasks.json` for a real build task) -- the process-lineage condition (write attributed to an npm-family process rather than an editor/IDE process itself) is the discriminator; if the log source cannot attribute file writes to a specific process image, this rule cannot be safely deployed as-is
CI scaffolding that generates one of these paths as part of a legitimate repository template/bootstrap step -- exclude by known-good CI runner identity
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=11 AND ((TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.claude\\setup.mjs' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.claude\\settings.json' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.gemini\\settings.json' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.vscode\\tasks.json' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.vscode\\setup.mjs' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%\\.github\\setup.js' ESCAPE '\') AND (Image LIKE '%\\node.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\npm.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\npm.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\npm-cli.js' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\pnpm.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\pnpm.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\yarn.cmd' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\yarn.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\bun.exe' ESCAPE '\')))
title: Miasma npm worm -- T1546 AI-assisted IDE config poisoning (Claude Code/Cursor/Gemini/VS Code)

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Vendor-disclosed detection for CVE-2026-48989 (GHSA-vrxg-gm77-7q5g,
CVSS 8.9 HIGH), a self-reported advisory for Windows-MCP, an open-source
project integrating AI agents with Windows via MCP.

Prior to 0.7.5, the SSE and Streamable-HTTP transport modes (the default
`stdio` mode is unaffected) configured `_http_middleware()` with wildcard
CORS -- `allow_origins=["*"]`, `allow_methods=["*"]`, `allow_headers=["*"]`
-- and exposed the MCP control plane without authentication at
`http://localhost:8000/mcp`. The same server registers a `PowerShell`
tool (`src/windows_mcp/tools/shell.py`) that forwards a caller-controlled
`command` argument to `PowerShellExecutor.execute_command`
(`src/windows_mcp/desktop/powershell.py`), which runs it via
`powershell -EncodedCommand`. Combined, any origin -- browser or
non-browser -- could reach the control plane and run arbitrary
PowerShell as the Windows user running Windows-MCP. The advisory's own
example call: `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":
{"name":"PowerShell","arguments":{"command":"calc.exe","timeout":30}}}`.

Detection logic flags the resulting HOST-side signal: a `powershell.exe`
process invoked with `-EncodedCommand`, whose parent process is the
Windows-MCP server rather than an interactive user shell or a scheduled
task -- the `-EncodedCommand` flag is the specific artifact of this
server's own execution path (base64-encoding the caller's command before
invocation), not a generic "PowerShell ran" heuristic.

Aggregated from 1 first-party vendor security advisory (CursorTouch, via
GHSA and NVD), fixed in 0.7.5.
falsepositives: A deployment already upgraded to 0.7.5+, where the control plane now requires authentication and no longer accepts wildcard-origin requests -- a matching process on a fixed deployment reflects legitimate, authenticated tool use, not exploitation of this specific bug

Legitimate operator use of the PowerShell tool through a correctly- authenticated MCP client, which also produces this exact process signature -- the parent-process condition narrows to Windows-MCP's own execution path, but cannot by itself distinguish an authorized caller from an attacker exploiting the wildcard-CORS/no-auth gap; correlate with the HTTP request's Origin header and auth state if the log source captures it
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=1 AND (((Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\pwsh.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\') AND ((ParentImage LIKE '%\\windows-mcp.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\windows\_mcp.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND ParentCommandLine LIKE '%windows\_mcp%' ESCAPE '\')))
title: Windows-MCP -- T1059.001 wildcard-CORS reachable PowerShell tool execution

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Real, actively-exploited-in-the-wild RMM authentication-bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-18577, an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-18556), added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog 2026-08-03 after N-able's own advisory disclosed in-the-wild exploitation since 2026-08-01. Cross-verified against two independent incident-response/threat-intel vendors (Huntress and Rapid7), which report matching post-exploitation artifacts -- not just the same narrative, the same specific indicators.

Post-auth-bypass, attackers abuse N-central's Take Control functionality (via the legitimate 'MSP Support' account) to reach managed downstream endpoints, then establish persistence via a Cloudflare Tunnel registered as a Windows service named 'Cloudflared', alongside a suspicious svchost.exe binary planted in the compromised user's Documents folder -- masquerading as the legitimate Windows svchost.exe, which never legitimately runs from a user profile path.

Verification discipline: both artifacts below (Documents-folder svchost.exe, Cloudflared service name) appear identically in both Huntress's and Rapid7's independent write-ups. The network IOCs both sources also list (a handful of static IPs) are deliberately excluded from this rule's detection logic -- both sources themselves note most of those IPs resolve to shared Mullvad/NordVPN exit-node infrastructure, not attacker-exclusive hosting, so encoding them here would be a high-false-positive/low-specificity signal rather than a real detection.
falsepositives: Legitimate, sanctioned use of Cloudflare Tunnel for remote access elsewhere in the environment -- verify against a known-tunnel inventory before escalating on the Cloudflared selection alone
A user manually saving or extracting an unrelated file literally named svchost.exe into Documents (rare, but not impossible) -- the real distinguishing signal is execution, not presence
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=1 AND ((Image LIKE '%\\Documents\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\svchost.exe' ESCAPE '\') OR (CommandLine LIKE '%cloudflared%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%Cloudflared%' ESCAPE '\')))
title: N-able N-central CVE-2026-18577 exploitation -- svchost masquerade + Cloudflared persistence (2026-08-02)

author: WRG-11
description:
Detects the persistence mechanism of the Photo ZIP campaign reported by
Microsoft on 2026-06-25 (unattributed; hospitality-sector phishing that
delivers a Node.js implant). The campaign persists by writing an HKCU Run or
RunOnce value that launches a JavaScript payload staged under
AppData\Local\Nodejs, alongside a second RunOnce value that launches a PE
under ProgramData and is refreshed on each execution.

Detection logic flags a Run or RunOnce registry value whose data references a
user-space Node.js path (AppData\Local\Nodejs) or a node.exe launch of a
local .js file. A user profile auto-starting node.exe against a local script
out of a Run key is uncommon outside this implant; pair with the campaign C2
indicators (for example the .cfd photo-NNNN domains or the documented C2 IPs)
for confirmation.

Authored from the published Microsoft advisory, not from synthetic content.
falsepositives: Legitimate Node.js or Electron desktop applications that register a Run key auto-start; confirm the referenced path and the binary publisher before alerting.
Developer tooling that auto-starts a local Node script at logon; scope by user and by the AppData\Local\Nodejs path, which is specific to this implant.
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=13 AND ((TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\%' ESCAPE '\') AND (Details LIKE '%\\AppData\\Local\\Nodejs\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR Details LIKE '%node.exe%' ESCAPE '\')))
title: Photo ZIP campaign Node.js implant persistence via HKCU Run key -- T1547.001

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Detection for the chained CVE-2026-42248 + CVE-2026-42249 (cert.pl,
2026-04-29), affecting Ollama for Windows versions 0.12.10 through
0.17.5 (maintainers did not confirm the full vulnerable range when
notified).

Two independent bugs chain into unattended, persistent code execution.
First (CVE-2026-42248): unlike other platforms, Ollama for Windows'
update-verification routine unconditionally returns success -- no
digital signature or trust validation runs before an update payload is
staged or executed. Second (CVE-2026-42249): when downloading an
update, the client builds the local staging file path using values
taken from HTTP response headers, passed directly to `filepath.Join`
with no validation, so a header containing `../` traversal sequences
resolves outside the intended staging directory -- an attacker who can
influence the update response (e.g. positioned on the network path, or
controlling/spoofing the update endpoint) can write an arbitrary
executable to any location the current user can reach, including the
Windows Startup folder. Because Ollama for Windows performs SILENT
automatic updates with no user interaction, the two bugs together
deliver a malicious executable straight into Startup and it runs on
the next login with no signature check and no prompt.

Detection logic flags the resulting host-level artifact: a new
executable file created inside a user's Startup folder
(`...\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\`) by a process
attributed to Ollama's updater -- Ollama's own update mechanism has no
legitimate reason to place a NEW executable directly in Startup as part
of an ordinary in-place version update.

Aggregated from 1 independent technical write-up (cert.pl, a
CERT-affiliated vulnerability coordination body), citing both CVE
entries. No patched version was confirmed by the maintainers as of the
write-up's publication -- stated explicitly, not assumed.
falsepositives: No patched version was confirmed by the maintainers as of this rule's authoring, so this rule cannot rely on a fixed-deployment negative case the way most rules in this corpus do -- treat every match as needing manual review

A user or administrator legitimately using Ollama's own updater to place a shortcut/launcher in Startup by explicit configuration -- narrow in practice since ordinary Ollama updates replace the existing installed binary rather than adding a new Startup entry, but a log source that cannot distinguish "new Startup file" from "existing Startup file rewritten" may alias the two
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=11 AND ((TargetFilename LIKE '%\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND TargetFilename LIKE '%.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND Image LIKE '%ollama%' ESCAPE '\'))
title: Ollama for Windows -- T1547.001 unsigned update + header-driven path traversal writes to Startup

author: WRG-11
description:
Detects the on-disk artefacts GTIG reports for PROMPTFLUX, a VBScript
dropper that asks the Gemini API to rewrite its own source code and saves
the new, obfuscated version to the Startup folder for persistence. Its
"Thinking Robot" module periodically queries Gemini for new evasion code
and logs the model responses to %TEMP%\thinking_robot_log.txt.

Two observable surfaces are matched: the response log file name reported
by GTIG, and a Windows Script Host process writing a script into a Startup
folder. The log file name is a family-specific indicator and can be
changed by the author; the Startup write is the behavioural surface that
survives renaming, because a metamorphic script must still persist
somewhere it will be re-launched.

GTIG does not attribute PROMPTFLUX to a named threat actor and describes
the observed samples as experimental.
falsepositives: Login scripts that a Windows Script Host job deliberately copies into a user Startup folder; allowlist the known script names.
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=11 AND (TargetFilename LIKE '%\\thinking\_robot\_log.txt' ESCAPE '\' OR ((Image LIKE '%\\wscript.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\cscript.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND (TargetFilename LIKE '%\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND (TargetFilename LIKE '%.vbs' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%.vbe' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetFilename LIKE '%.js' ESCAPE '\')))))
title: PROMPTFLUX -- LLM self-regeneration artefacts of a VBScript dropper -- T1027

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from StepSecurity disclosure)
description:
Campaign-bound sigma detection for the nx-console VS Code extension supply chain compromise (StepSecurity disclosure 2026-05-18; nrwl.angular-console v18.95.0 approximately 11-minute malicious window). Attack chain:
(1) Orphan commit payload published from the official nrwl/nx GitHub repository, appearing legitimate at install time. (2) Post-install multi-stage credential stealer harvests GitHub tokens, npm tokens, AWS keys, HashiCorp Vault tokens, kubeconfig files, and 1Password vault items. (3) Triple-channel exfiltration over HTTPS, GitHub API write, and DNS tunneling (3 independent egress paths to defeat single-channel block lists).
NOVEL: First-of-kind Sigstore provenance bypass -- attackers used stolen npm OIDC tokens to request Fulcio certificate issuance and produce SLSA provenance attestations, breaking the industry-wide signature-trust assumption for the ecosystem. Sigma rule flags VS Code extension install events targeting nrwl.angular-console at affected versions, plus suspicious child processes spawned from the extension host (PowerShell / curl / wget / node egress to api.github.com or non-standard DNS resolvers after extension install).
Related rules: Nx campaign cluster -- Mini Shai-Hulud npm + s1ngularity CLI + ClawHavoc Claude Skills + nx-console VS Code. Cross-reference observed_mini_shai_hulud_npm_supply_chain_c2_t1071.yml, observed_s1ngularity_nx_npm_token_exfil_t1195_002.yml, and observed_clawhavoc_claude_skills_t1195_002.yml in the same corpus.
Source: multi-source disclosure (StepSecurity blog 2026-05-18 direct; amplified by industry reporting). Aggregated from 1 first-party StepSecurity disclosure 2026-05-18.
falsepositives: Legitimate developer install of nrwl.angular-console at safe versions (not v18.95.0; verify version pin against StepSecurity disclosure window) -- tune CommandLine substring to include affected version marker
Developer-tool egress to api.github.com is normal for project workflow -- combine parent-image VS Code filter AND credential-file substring to reduce noise
Legitimate Sigstore signing workflow (cosign / rekor) by your own release pipelines -- exclude known build identities from the selection_sigstore_artifact_indicator selection
Review for environment-specific tuning before deployment

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules
description: Detects sc.exe creating a Windows service whose binary path points to the typosquatted host scvhost.exe, or whose svchost service group is WinMainSvc or MSRuntime. Trend Micro documented Crypto24 operators on victim Windows hosts running "sc create WinMainSvc type= share start= auto binPath= C:\Windows\System32\scvhost.exe -k WinMainSvc" for a keylogger service and "sc create MSRuntime type= share start= auto binpath= C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -k MSRuntime" for the ransomware service. The rule matches that service-creation behaviour, not the actor name; a hit is evidence of this masquerade, not proof of Crypto24 involvement.
falsepositives: An in-house or third-party installer that registers a svchost-hosted service under a group literally named WinMainSvc or MSRuntime; confirm the service DLL's publisher and signature before closing
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=1 AND ((Image LIKE '%\\sc.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '% create %' ESCAPE '\') AND (CommandLine LIKE '%\\scvhost.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR (CommandLine LIKE '%-k WinMainSvc%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%-k MSRuntime%' ESCAPE '\'))))
title: Crypto24 -- Service Created With a Masqueraded svchost Host or a Documented Crypto24 Service Group

author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Real, actively-exploited-as-a-zero-day on-premises SharePoint Server deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-58644, CVSS 9.8), confirmed by Microsoft's own advisory and added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog 2026-07-16 (agencies given a 3-day remediation deadline). Post-exploitation activity including IIS machine-key theft and malware deployment is documented in Microsoft's and CISA's advisories.

Verification discipline: multiple independent write-ups covering this specific CVE (Rapid7, Resecurity) DISAGREE on -- or in Rapid7's case, explicitly state as not yet publicly disclosed -- the exact vulnerable endpoint path and webshell filenames some secondary sources list (several of those specifics match the well-known, prior 'ToolShell' SharePoint chain from 2025 and may be conflated with it rather than confirmed for this CVE). Those specifics are deliberately NOT encoded here.

What IS independently corroborated across sources for this exploitation wave, and is also simply how this CVE class works mechanically (the deserialization payload executes inside the IIS worker process): w3wp.exe spawning a command shell or script-interpreter child process, particularly PowerShell invoked with an encoded/obfuscated command flag -- a legitimate SharePoint worker process has no normal reason to spawn any of these.
falsepositives: SharePoint farm administration scripts or approved third-party web parts that legitimately shell out from the IIS worker process -- rare, but confirm against a documented baseline before dismissing a hit
Endpoint/EDR agents that inject monitoring child processes under IIS worker processes
rule: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Channel='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' AND (EventID=1 AND ((ParentImage LIKE '%\\w3wp.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (Image LIKE '%\\cmd.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\pwsh.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\csc.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\cscript.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\wscript.exe' ESCAPE '\')) OR (ParentImage LIKE '%\\w3wp.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%-enc %' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%-ec %' ESCAPE '\'))))
title: SharePoint Server CVE-2026-58644 RCE -- w3wp.exe spawning a shell/script interpreter (2026-07)
